extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, literary critics, and educated readers interested in dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical criteria for composing English tragic drama (verse, plot, character, and rhetorical choices), drawn from early-18th-century literary criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer blank verse for English tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank verse is the most proper measure for Tragedy in English because it lifts discourse above prose while remaining close to ordinary speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing a play in rhyme; a Play in Rhyme in English is compared to a Tragedy of Hexameters in Greek or Latin and is called absurd. Blank verse is a due medium between rhyme and prose and is wonderfully adapted to Tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix rhyme and blank verse within the same play
rubrics_metrics.description: Having some scenes in Rhyme and some in Blank Verse is a solecism: they are 'two several Languages'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing the two creates an incoherent linguistic register; if rhyme is used it should be deliberate and not interspersed arbitrarily with blank verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow occasional couplets at exits or act-ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may conclude a Tragedy, or every Act of it, with two or three couplets to give a graceful exit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can have the effect of an Italian opera's air after a recitative; brevity and measured use of couplets are advised rather than pervasive rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a diversity of metrical numbers to avoid tiring the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of Numbers in parts of a play hinders the ear from being tired with the same continued modulation of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary rhythms and line lengths (e.g., occasional hemistichs or different metrical devices) to maintain auditory interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemistichs and abrupt pauses are acceptable when motivated by passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches that close with a hemistick or abrupt break are permissible, provided they humour the passion being expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices may heighten emotion and are allowable even when a new verse begins without filling the prior one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise noble thought over ornate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble sentiment with homely language is preferable to a vulgar thought dressed in sonorous, blown-up expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the idea itself merits the eloquence — do not use grand language to conceal weak or common thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose the dialogue in plain English before versifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay down the whole contexture of dialogue in plain English before turning it into blank verse so the naked thought of every speech can be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps to prevent being 'imposed upon by Words' and allows impartial judgement of whether a thought is natural and great enough for the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscuring strong thoughts with pompous phrases and hard metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Great and just thoughts are often obscured by sounding phrases, hard metaphors, and forced expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep expression clear in passionate parts; reserve elaborate phrasing for descriptive or unactive passages where it may be laboured to effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour expression in unactive parts (descriptions, similitudes, narrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression ought to be much laboured in unactive parts of the fable — descriptions, similitudes, narrations — where opinions, manners and passions are not represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In descriptive sections, careful, artful phrasing is desirable; in passages representing passion or character, simplicity aids clarity of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match language register to the nature of the speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions, manners, and passions are apt to be obscured by pompous phrases; the expression must suit whether the passage is descriptive or a representation of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise language and dignity where the fable requires it; follow nature in passionate speech (as Otway does) and avoid undue pomp where naturalness is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure thoughts are appropriate to the speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a thought is natural or great enough for the person that utters it and whether it deserves such elaborate eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divest lines of their ornaments and judge the naked idea against the character and situation; do not let language inflate an unworthy thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain exuberant genius; keep the style within bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's impetuosity should be restrained and kept within proper bounds; ungoverned fire can be lost in a cloud of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel invention so that passion and force are visible rather than obscured by excessive metaphor and 'smoke'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow nature in passioned language to achieve sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poets who follow nature in the language of their tragedies shine in passionate parts; familiarity and domesticity can produce force without pomp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural speech often better conveys tenderness and pathos than overwrought diction; adapt register to the scene's emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose plots that elicit proper sympathy — heroic qualities must be placed rightly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid plots that make the greatest characters rebels and traitors; had the hero shown his virtues in a noble cause, his fall would be more admirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or shape fables so that the audience can properly pity and admire the principal characters; the moral orientation of the plot affects audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require poetical justice; unhappy endings can be stronger
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should not be bound to make virtue always triumphant; tragedies that end unhappily often produce greater terror and commiseration and were preferred by the ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a disastrous ending serves the primary design of raising pity and fear more effectively than contrived rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tragi-comedy mixing mirth and sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-Comedy, mixing mirth and sorrow in one piece, is called a monstrous invention and generally absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mixing tones, do it cautiously; the altred tide of emotions can dilute audience concern for the principal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of double plots; ensure under-plot closely relates to main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Double plots can divert grief and weaken concern for the principal action unless the under-plot bears a near relation and contributes towards completion and shares the same catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an under-plot that mirrors or reinforces the main design rather than distracting the audience with unrelated sorrow or comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing 'rants' — bombast, unnatural exclamations, and forced vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rants' — unnatural exclamations, curses, vows, blasphemies, and outraging of the gods — often pass for towering thoughts but are really bombast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not inflate language to produce applause; true greatness of sentiment need not be clothed in fustian. Beware of composing lines aimed merely at eliciting loud audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to vulgar stage-tastes that favour inconsistent hero behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: A device of making a hero insolent toward men and abject toward his mistress may win favour with certain audiences but can be a false beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shaping character chiefly to court the applause of particular audience segments; maintain consistent, credible character behaviour even if it costs momentary popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray affectation as a fault in character and avoid it in depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation — self-conscious effort to show off in look, word, and gesture — turns beauty and wit into deformity and absurdity; it betrays an interrupted consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters (and real persons) should be shown as focused on main purposes rather than constantly seeking praise; avoid writing mannered postures or speech that signal vanity rather than genuine feeling or motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character authenticity comes from focus on central aims, not self-conscious display
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters' thoughts are fixed upon chief purposes in business or pleasure they do not betray affectation; a thorough disregard to petty particulars allows laudable sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show characters engaged in meaningful objectives — this produces natural action and speech; petty self-regard in small matters is to be avoided in credible depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend reading that enlightens understanding and rectifies the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: For the improvement of readers (especially women, in the essay's context), prefer books that enlighten the understanding and rectify the passions over those that merely divert the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and recommenders should select works with moral and intellectual improvement as aims, not solely entertainment; this is presented as a criterion for 'useful' reading.
